title: Understanding the Experience of the Visually Impaired towards a Multi-Sensorial Architectural Design

findings.antecedent: spending time outside (nature interaction)
findings.consequent: preference for outside
findings.quote: Downey... mentioned that he prefers to spend more time outside.

findings.antecedent: outside environment (breezes, sounds of leaves, birds, street life)
findings.consequent: dynamic experience and enjoyment
findings.mechanism: Multi-sensory input (breezes, sounds) creates a dynamic and enjoyable experience.
findings.quote: The outside is so much more dynamic. There are breezes... enjoying the street life and all the sounds.

findings.antecedent: sun heat on skin, air heat, air flow (thermal/airflow sensations)
findings.consequent: understanding atmosphere and feeling light intensity
findings.mechanism: Tactile/thermal sensations provide information about light and atmosphere.
findings.quote: the only way that I could feel the light intensity in a space was feeling the sun heat on my skin...

findings.antecedent: sound of pelting rain
findings.consequent: interpreting contour of land, understanding hill curvature, sense of being in the room (spatial understanding)
findings.mechanism: Auditory cues from rain provide spatial information.
findings.quote: through the sound of pelting rain I can interpret the contour of the land...

findings.antecedent: calmness, birds, water stream, air penetrating through grass and leaves, smelling plants and water, sunlight warmth, smell of greens, flowers, water stream blending in with soil and rocks, splashing on rocks (multi-sensory natural elements)
findings.consequent: recognition of tree shaded areas, feeling of freshness, blending in with natural elements (spatial recognition, positive affect)
findings.mechanism: Combination of auditory, olfactory, thermal, and haptic sensations from nature provides rich environmental information and a sense of connection.
findings.quote: Entering the park from the main street and feeling the sudden calmness, only hearing birds, water stream...

findings.antecedent: touching, tapping, listening to echoes of materials
findings.consequent: materials are felt and understood
findings.mechanism: Haptic and auditory feedback from materials provides information about their properties.
findings.quote: Materials are felt... They are heard and felt through touching, tapping and listening to their echoes.

findings.antecedent: rain striking concrete, rain drumming into trees, rain on large bush (different material surfaces)
findings.consequent: different sounds, understanding earth falling on road, swish of cars (material recognition, spatial awareness)
findings.mechanism: Auditory cues from rain interacting with different surfaces provide information about materials and spatial features.
findings.quote: When the rain is striking the concrete, here it is splashing into the shallow pools which have already formed.

findings.antecedent: rough asphalt, smooth lawn, smooth path, concrete pavers (material texture contrast)
findings.consequent: material recognition
findings.mechanism: Haptic contrast between materials aids recognition.
findings.quote: The contrast between the rough asphalt and the smooth lawn was very recognized...

findings.antecedent: using feet to feel floor materials, stretching leg to identify objects, feeling different textures (haptic exploration)
findings.consequent: identifying objects, knowing exact location, material recognition (spatial awareness, object recognition)
findings.mechanism: Haptic feedback from feet and legs provides information about floor materials and object locations.
findings.quote: Visually impaired children are trained to use their feet to feel floor materials under them...

findings.antecedent: duplicates of wood, metal, plastic and concrete (different materials)
findings.consequent: recognizing them from their texture, temperature and weight, matching same materials (material recognition)
findings.mechanism: Haptic (texture, temperature, weight) feedback allows material identification.
findings.quote: The children learn to identify different materials through a Montessori activity where they use duplicates of wood, metal, plastic and concrete...

findings.antecedent: metal vs wood (material type)
findings.consequent: recognized by 'cold, smooth and heavy' vs 'rough, warm and light' (material properties)
findings.mechanism: Haptic properties (temperature, texture, weight) differentiate materials.
findings.quote: The children recognized metal by asking about the 'cold, smooth and heavy' material, comparing it to wood...

findings.antecedent: dead acoustics (lack of sound)
findings.consequent: things didn't quite come together, couldn't understand form of spaces (lack of spatial understanding)
findings.mechanism: Lack of auditory feedback hinders spatial comprehension.
findings.quote: My first experience was going there without sight, and some things didn't quite come together, like the acoustics.

findings.antecedent: opening door, cane hit concrete floor, people walking on crushed gravel pathways, sound of fountain (auditory cues)
findings.consequent: hear architecture, hear whole length extend, delightful space (spatial understanding, positive affect)
findings.mechanism: Rich auditory environment provides spatial information and positive experience.
findings.quote: As soon as I opened the door and my cane hit the concrete floor, I could hear the architecture. I could hear the whole length extend out in either direction.

findings.antecedent: hearing (auditory perception)
findings.consequent: imagined height, sense of distance, identify location and orientation (spatial understanding)
findings.mechanism: Auditory cues provide information about distance, height, location, and orientation.
findings.quote: Architecture is how he imagined and understood the space, it is how he imagined the height because hearing is the sense of distance...

findings.antecedent: echo (auditory cue)
findings.consequent: understanding space wideness, how crowded it is (spatial understanding)
findings.mechanism: Echo provides information about spatial dimensions and occupancy.
findings.quote: Echo used to play a very important role in understanding the surrounding space, it made me understand the space wideness and how crowded it is...

findings.antecedent: high echo
findings.consequent: space is wide and empty (spatial understanding)
findings.mechanism: High echo correlates with large, empty spaces.
findings.quote: high echo means a space is wide and empty and vice versa.

findings.antecedent: low ceilings
findings.consequent: high echoes (auditory property)
findings.mechanism: Ceiling height affects reverberation.
findings.quote: low ceilings result in high echoes

findings.antecedent: high ceilings
findings.consequent: hard to track echo (auditory property)
findings.mechanism: High ceilings can diffuse sound, making echo tracking difficult.
findings.quote: high ceilings make it hard to track echo

findings.antecedent: place without echoes (acoustic property)
findings.consequent: dead place (negative affect, lack of liveliness)
findings.mechanism: Lack of auditory feedback makes a space feel lifeless.
findings.quote: a place without echoes is a dead place for him.

findings.antecedent: carpeted airports (material, acoustic property)
findings.consequent: dead and flat, never heard footfalls or roller bags, no liveliness (negative affect, lack of spatial information)
findings.mechanism: Carpeting absorbs sound, reducing auditory cues that convey liveliness and activity.
findings.quote: Carpeted airports... It was dead and flat. You never heard footfalls or roller bags...

findings.antecedent: sound of travel, sound of people moving around (auditory cues)
findings.consequent: excitement in the space, liveliness (positive affect, spatial understanding)
findings.mechanism: Auditory cues from activity convey liveliness and excitement.
findings.quote: It's because you can hear the sound of travel, the sound of people moving around

findings.antecedent: walk around, touch surroundings with cane, hands, feet, hit objects, clap to feel echo, smell materials (multi-sensory exploration)
findings.consequent: identify and understand a place, wideness of space, develop mental map, easier to understand when revisited (spatial understanding, memory)
findings.mechanism: Active multi-sensory exploration builds a comprehensive mental map.
findings.quote: To be able to identify and understand a place, I walk around, touch the surroundings with my cane, hands and feet...

findings.antecedent: sound echo higher (auditory cue)
findings.consequent: understanding how wide the street was, recognized street (spatial understanding, recognition)
findings.mechanism: Auditory echo provides information about street width.
findings.quote: the sound echo was higher, this helped in understanding how wide the street was...

findings.antecedent: smell of perfumes, incenses, bakeries and coffee (olfactory cues)
findings.consequent: remembered specific areas (spatial memory, recognition)
findings.mechanism: Olfactory cues act as spatial markers for memory.
findings.quote: The scent along the walk was important as participants remembered specific areas through the smell of perfumes...

findings.antecedent: touch surrounding walls (haptic exploration)
findings.consequent: identify location and buildings (spatial recognition)
findings.mechanism: Haptic feedback from walls aids in identifying locations and buildings.
findings.quote: it was very important to touch the surrounding walls to be able to identify the location and buildings...

findings.antecedent: sunlight penetrating through windows, warmth on skin (thermal/light sensation)
findings.consequent: easy to indicate locations of windows (spatial recognition)
findings.mechanism: Thermal and light sensations provide cues for window locations.
findings.quote: the sunlight penetrating through the windows was felt on our skin and its warmth made it easy to indicate the locations of windows...

findings.antecedent: approaching double-heighted staircase area, moving towards main entrance where door opens and closes (spatial configuration, airflow)
findings.consequent: airflow felt higher (haptic/thermal sensation)
findings.mechanism: Airflow changes with spatial configuration and openings.
findings.quote: the airflow felt higher when approaching the double-heighted staircase area and moving towards the main entrance...

findings.antecedent: using arms and feet to recognize walls, doors, chairs, table, objects (haptic exploration)
findings.consequent: identify spaces, recognize objects (spatial recognition, object recognition)
findings.mechanism: Active haptic exploration helps in identifying objects and spatial boundaries.
findings.quote: arms and feet are used to recognize walls, doors, chairs, table and all other objects.

findings.antecedent: touching an obstructing rope (haptic interaction)
findings.consequent: identify and avoid obstacles (behavioral skill)
findings.mechanism: Haptic feedback from obstacles trains avoidance behavior.
findings.quote: achieved by touching an obstructing rope and reacting to it (Fig. 3).

findings.antecedent: reaching rope becomes harder, new, unrecognized spaces with unknown obstacles (environmental challenge)
findings.consequent: feel that they can fall anytime, hardest activities (negative affect, difficulty)
findings.mechanism: Uncertainty and difficulty in obstacle avoidance lead to fear and perceived difficulty.
findings.quote: children feel that they can fall anytime when reaching the rope becomes harder...

findings.antecedent: imagined things before surgery vs seen things after surgery
findings.consequent: not different, same but with colors (cognitive consistency)
findings.mechanism: Mental representations formed through other senses are robust and consistent with visual input, except for color.
findings.quote: It was not different, it was the same but with colors". Everything that he imagined became almost as it is.

findings.antecedent: touching and feeling object attributes (haptic exploration)
findings.consequent: knowing object identity when seeing it (object recognition)
findings.mechanism: Haptic memory and experience facilitate visual object recognition.
findings.quote: When I saw the table, I knew that this was a table because I remember touching and feeling it, just like seeing it".

findings.antecedent: shaping play dough into spheres, cubes, rods, touching and naming shapes (haptic-motor activity)
findings.consequent: perceive size and shape of objects, assures object's name (object recognition, cognitive understanding)
findings.mechanism: Active haptic and motor engagement with objects develops stereognosis and object recognition.
findings.quote: children shape the play dough into spheres, cubes and rods. Once they form the shape, they touch it and name it...

findings.antecedent: touch and feel objects, arrange from big to small, train to recognize different weights (haptic exploration, comparative tasks)
findings.consequent: understand different forms, recognize objects, full understanding of what sizes mean, recognize different weights (object recognition, cognitive understanding of properties)
findings.mechanism: Haptic exploration and comparative tasks develop understanding of object properties like form, size, scale, and weight.
findings.quote: visually impaired children touch and feel the objects to be able to recognize them. They also need to learn that there is something called size and scale...

findings.antecedent: arranging spheres and cubes on a rod (haptic-motor activity)
findings.consequent: understand different forms, activate tactile sense (object recognition, sensory activation)
findings.mechanism: Manipulating objects haptically develops form understanding and tactile sensitivity.
findings.quote: arranging forms on a rod... It is a way to understand the different forms and activate the tactile sense.

findings.antecedent: touching rods of different scales, arranging them from longest to shortest (haptic-motor activity)
findings.consequent: learn about scale and proportion (cognitive understanding)
findings.mechanism: Haptic exploration and ordering tasks develop understanding of scale and proportion.
findings.quote: visually impaired children learn about scale and proportion by touching rods of different scales and arranging them from longest to shortest.

findings.antecedent: arranging rings based on size (haptic-motor activity)
findings.consequent: learn about scale and proportion (cognitive understanding)
findings.mechanism: Haptic exploration and ordering tasks develop understanding of scale and proportion.
findings.quote: arranging rings, the children arrange rings based on their size from the biggest to the smallest.

findings.antecedent: haptic feedback, touching sense
findings.consequent: perceive surrounding environment, feel nature, feel space, recognize space, recognize materials (environmental perception, recognition)
findings.mechanism: Haptic input provides direct information about environmental properties.
findings.quote: Haptic feedback is one of the main channels through which the visually impaired perceive their surrounding environment.

findings.antecedent: active touching (moving, exerting pressure, pushing, pulling), materials texture identification, feeling ground contours, form recognition, object parameter feeling, form generation/identification (active haptic exploration)
findings.consequent: select and refine sensations, appropriate perceptual information (enhanced perception, information gathering)
findings.mechanism: Active engagement with the environment through touch allows for selective and refined sensory input.
findings.quote: Through active touching, visually impaired people select and refine the sensations to give the appropriate perceptual information...

findings.antecedent: passive touching (heat sensation, feeling nature, airflow, splashing water)
findings.consequent: feel light intensity, feel nature surrounding (environmental perception)
findings.mechanism: Unexpected tactile/thermal events provide information about the environment.
findings.quote: Passive touching happens when a tactile event occurs that is unexpectedly reaching the body.

findings.antecedent: tactile palette, tactile visual border, contrast between two materials in texture (design features)
findings.consequent: clear distinction (material recognition)
findings.mechanism: Tactile contrast enhances material differentiation for visually impaired users.
findings.quote: A contrast between two materials should be clear in its texture [5].

findings.antecedent: hearing (auditory perception)
findings.consequent: perceive and understand surrounding world, three-dimensional distant and near atmosphere (spatial understanding)
findings.mechanism: Auditory cues provide spatial information, especially for distance and depth.
findings.quote: Hearing is crucial for the visually impaired to perceive and understand their surrounding world...

findings.antecedent: sound of nature, acoustic experience of rain (auditory natural elements)
findings.consequent: preferred, blend with surrounding environment, mentally understand surrounding environment (positive affect, spatial understanding)
findings.mechanism: Natural sounds provide a sense of connection and spatial information.
findings.quote: The sound of nature is usually preferred to by the visually impaired because it makes them blend with the surrounding environment...

findings.antecedent: sounds of activity (auditory cues)
findings.consequent: dynamic place, liveliness (positive affect, spatial quality)
findings.mechanism: Auditory cues from activity convey a sense of dynamism and liveliness.
findings.quote: The term "dynamic place" was mentioned by Chris Downey while describing a place with sounds of activity...

findings.antecedent: carpeted places (material, acoustic property)
findings.consequent: does not hear liveliness, dead (negative affect, lack of spatial quality)
findings.mechanism: Carpeting reduces sounds of activity, making a place feel lifeless.
findings.quote: unlike "carpeted places" where he does not hear the liveliness of the place, and so he described it as dead.

findings.antecedent: sound echo, sound of materials (from cane tapping) (auditory cues)
findings.consequent: materials and spatial recognition (recognition)
findings.mechanism: Echo and material sounds provide information for recognition.
findings.quote: Sound echo also helps in materials and spatial recognition...

findings.antecedent: sense of smell (olfactory perception)
findings.consequent: build mental representation of surrounding environment (cognitive mapping)
findings.mechanism: Olfactory cues contribute to the formation of mental maps.
findings.quote: sense of smell helps visually impaired people build a mental representation of their surrounding environment.

findings.antecedent: sense of smell (olfactory perception)
findings.consequent: related to emotions and memory (affective and cognitive response)
findings.mechanism: Olfactory system has strong connections to limbic system, influencing emotion and memory.
findings.quote: sense of smell is how it is related to emotions and memory.

findings.antecedent: certain smell of a place, smell of materials (wood, plaster, paint, damp concrete) (olfactory cues)
findings.consequent: places easily identified, recalled when revisited, materials identified, age of material recognized (spatial recognition, memory, material recognition)
findings.mechanism: Distinct smells act as identifiers and memory triggers for places and materials.
findings.quote: Places were easily identified with smell because every place has a certain smell that can be recalled when revisited...

findings.antecedent: harmony between haptic, auditory and olfactory perceptions, senses synchronization (multisensory integration)
findings.consequent: successful orientation and mobility, easily recognize familiar environments (spatial navigation, recognition)
findings.mechanism: Integrated multisensory input provides comprehensive environmental information for navigation and recognition.
findings.quote: For successful orientation and mobility of the visually impaired, a harmony between haptic, auditory and olfactory perceptions is achieved...

findings.antecedent: targeted training of spatial mental mapping, using all senses (intervention, multisensory engagement)
findings.consequent: enhance cognitive mapping skills, move safely and independently (cognitive skill, behavioral outcome)
findings.mechanism: Multisensory training improves cognitive mapping, leading to better navigation.
findings.quote: visually impaired children learn to enhance their cognitive mapping skills by using all their senses to be able to move safely and independently.

stimuli.description: Outdoor environments in Weimar city (park, main street, specific buildings like Bauhaus University), Old Cairo streets and buildings, indoor exercise at Bauhaus University.
Montessori activity classroom in an NGO.
Montessori activity materials (obstructing ropes, play dough, spheres, cubes, rods, rings of different sizes, duplicates of wood, metal, plastic, concrete).
stimuli.source: text, Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 5, Fig. 6, Fig. 7

tables.description: Profiles of 5 visually impaired participants (age, gender, condition).
Summary of extracted themes, sub-themes, and associated perceptual channels (haptic, auditory, olfactory).
